stories.title: Three children, teacher killed in US school shooting
stories.summary: A 16-year-old opened fire at a school in the US killing four people, including three children, before being killed by an armed member of the community. The shooter entered Silver Rail Elementary School in Bend, Oregon by firing through locked doors, police said, without offering any details beyond the suspect's age. The dead were children aged five, eight and 11 and one teacher. In addition, a seven-year-old student and a 54-year-old teacher were taken to hospital with critical injuries, Bend Police Chief Mike Krantz told a press conference. Chief Krantz said a community member, whom he did not identify, saw the suspect enter the school and pursued him. Oregon Governor Tina Kotek, appearing at the same briefing, thanked the community member who "heroically intervened to stop further loss of life". "No parent should have to have this kind of day, and no community should have to live through this ‌kind of day. And as we learn more ⁠about the children and the adults who have been killed or injured, and their families and their loved ones, we are going to do a lot of crying, and we are going to cry together, and we're probably going to cry privately," she said.

stories.title: Donaldson 'deserves every day' of sentence, says DUP
stories.summary: Jeffrey Donaldson "deserves every day of the lengthy prison service he has to serve", the Democratic Unionist Party has said. Donaldson, the former leader of the party, was jailed for 15 years for the rape and sexual assault of a schoolgirl and the indecent assault of a second young girl for a series of historical sex offences. In a statement, the DUP said: "Today justice has been done with the sentencing of Jeffrey Donaldson for his vile and disgusting crimes against his victims. "Our first thoughts are again with the innocent victims, who having suffered such evil, were re-traumatised through giving evidence at the trial. "They deserve our compassion, support and respect. We hope they can find some measure of comfort and can look ahead to a new chapter in their lives." The party added: "Regardless of status or position every individual must be held accountable for their actions.

stories.title: Uisce Éireann CEO defends €118,000 pay rise
stories.summary: Uisce Éireann CEO Niall Gleeson has defended a €118,000 increase in his overall salary to €391,953 - saying he and the utility are providing value for money to the public. Mr Gleeson was asked about the pay rise during the latest meeting of the Dáil Public Accounts Committee, amid separate questions over a €4,000 spend on PR advice before attending the meeting with TDs and senators. During a robust exchange, Sinn Féin TD Cathy Bennett told Mr Gleeson, "I have to say you must be doing an amazing job" because his salary has increased by €118,000, a rise first reported in July. Ms Bennett compared the rise to the far smaller increase being sought by public sector workers taking part in nationwide strikes, before asking: "How does someone receive that increase in one year?" The Sinn Féin TD said, "I don't know how you can sit here and condone it [the salary]", referencing problems some of her constituents in Co Monaghan have in terms of accessing clean water, water connections, and water that is not "brown". In response, Mr Gleeson said his pay rise was agreed after "an independent review of all salaries" at utilities, and that "the board [of Uisce Éireann] took the recommendations" and agreed to them.

stories.title: France, Germany deal to safeguard European car industry
stories.summary: France and Germany confirmed today that they had reached a deal aimed at protecting Europe's struggling automotive sector, with agreements on the flashpoint issues of EU car emissions and "made in Europe" components. The pact, which is likely to shape European Union policy going forward, envisages further relaxing of CO2 emission rules and the inclusion of Britain in a public procurement scheme to bolster European car industries. "Our shared ambition is clear: to successfully transform our automotive industry while maintaining our climate ambition and ensuring that the cars of the future are produced in Europe," the French and German governments said in a statement. Paris and Berlin had been at loggerheads on the course Europe should take as it tries to revive a sector that accounts for 13 million jobs and 7% of the bloc's collective GDP. Germany wanted less stringent carbon emission targets for carmakers and a broad interpretation of "made in Europe" requirements to include key non-EU trade partners. France had pushed to preserve the bloc's climate ambitions and to keep the "made in Europe" public procurement scheme the purview of EU nations.

stories.title: Ukraine will keep hitting Russian refineries - Zelensky
stories.summary:
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky has said his country would resume hitting Russian oil refineries. US President Donald Trump last week unilaterally announced an "energy ceasefire" that was never publicly confirmed, and Russia continued striking Ukrainian energy infrastructure. After a wave of renewed Russian strikes on facilities yesterday, Mr Zelensky told the Financial Times: "The block (on attacking refineries) is out. We're done." Since Mr Trump returned to power, Washington's support for Ukraine has fluctuated alongside his unexpected social media remarks, which have often taken Russia and Ukraine by surprise.

Russia said this morning that Ukraine had attacked an oil refinery in Ryazan, south of the capital, Moscow. However, President Vladimir Putin said that recent Ukrainian strikes on Russian oil refineries had not caused significant damage and vowed that Moscow would respond, Interfax reported. "They hit here and there. Nothing particularly significant. Nevertheless they are carrying on," Mr Putin said.

stories.title: Huge blow for Donegal as Roarty signs for Collingwood
stories.summary: Donegal manager Jim McGuinness has been dealt a huge blow with the news that 2025 Young Footballer of the Year Finnbarr Roarty has signed a two-year rookie contract with Collingwood in the AFL. The 20-year-old will jet off to Australia at the end of the month to hook up with the Magpies, who finished in ninth place in last season's Premiership. Before all of that, the versatile defender will first look to push his club Naomh Conaill over the line in Sunday’s Donegal SFC final against St Eunan’s in Ballybofey. McGuinness, in his first game in charge back at the helm in 2024, threw the then 17-year-old in the mix against Armagh in the Dr McKenna Cup. However, it would soon transpire that the Glenties native’s inclusion broke a rule which stated that senior inter-county players have to be aged 18 by the start of the calendar year. The breaks were immediately pumped on that progression, but the very next season, Roarty would hit the ground running, winning an Ulster title and playing a huge part as Donegal raced all the way to the All-Ireland SFC final. It’s a serious blow for Donegal, though, as one of their main players becomes the latest rising Gaelic football star to depart Down Under.

stories.title: Strikers coming to the boil at business end of the season
stories.summary: Football is a sport that is constantly evolving. The old adage that winning a league title requires a 20-goal striker is starting to gather dust. No player has reached that mark in the last five seasons, not even surpassing 15 goals in that time. The average goals scored by the top scorer of the league champions in the last four years is 10.5. While no individual is putting up title-swaying numbers, strikers for this season's top three teams have all found ways to contribute timely goals to boost their sides as the title race reaches its apex. Goalscoring has been much improved across the league this year going up to an average of 2.78 per game, the most since 2018. Much of that has been fuelled by the top three upping their scoring rates in the final third of the season. A good deal of these improvements can be attributed to centre forwards for each team finding a new level of performance namely Colm Whelan, Aidan Keena and John McGovern. While Bohs' title hopes took a major hit with the result against Shamrock Rovers on Monday night, it had looked highly unlikely they would even enter that last month with a shot at the title. A loss to Dundalk on 19 June left them nine points behind Shamrock Rovers in fourth place.

stories.title: Edogbo signs new contract up to 2029
stories.summary: Munster and Ireland second-row Edwin Edogbo has signed a new two-year contract with the province and the IRFU that will see him remain in red until 2029. The 23-year-old made his Ireland debut back in February's Six Nations win over Italy, and has become a vital cog in Clayton McMillan's team since returning from successive long-term injuries across 2024 and early 2025. Having come through the ranks with Cobh Pirates, Edogbo was the first player from Cobh to enter the Munster academy back in 2021, and was soon followed by younger brother Seán. The lock made his Munster debut away to the Dragons in 2022, making eight appearances in their URC title winning season that same season. After missing all of the 2024/25 season through injury, Edogbo made his long-awaited return to the fold last year, making 16 appearances as well as his Champions Cup debut and later his Ireland debut. Speaking of the news, Munster head coach spoke of Edogbo's unique physical abilitiy.

stories.title: Damien Rice to return with 25 Years; 25 Cities tour
stories.summary: Irish singer songwriter Damien Rice will mark the 25th anniversary of the release of his celebrated debut album O with the 25 Years, 25 Cities tour, which includes two dates in Dublin in March. The 53-year-old Dubliner, who scored a massive cult hit with the album in 2002, will play Bord Gáis Energy Theatre on 21 and 22 March 2027, with tickets on sale on the 23 of October. Released in February 2002, O featured hit singles The Blower's Daughter, Cannonball, and Delicate and its deeply confessional songs and stripped-back sound spawned a whole new generation of singer songwriters, including Ed Sheeran, who has often cited it as a huge influence on his early work. Written, recorded, and produced at home, the album was praised for its DIY ethic and was funded by a loan from his father that needn't be repaid if the record was finished. The album features singer Lisa Hannigan and cellist Vyvienne Long. Rice says he was inspired to make the record after the support and belief of his second cousin, the composer David Arnold. However, he initially thought it would be the only album he'd ever make. It went on to be No 2 hit in Ireland and to win the Shortlist Prize for Artistic Achievement in Music, an award for albums that have sold less than 500,000 copies.

stories.title: Creative Director McGirr to leave McQueen after 3 years
stories.summary: Seán McGirr, the Dublin-born designer, is exiting storied fashion house McQueen after three years as the brand's Creative Director. Kering, the parent company of the London-based fashion house, made the annoucement today, just weeks after the brand's momentous return to the London Fashion Week circuit. McGirr joined McQueen in 2023, succeeding Sarah Burton, who took over as Creative Director in 2010 after the death of Lee Alexander McQueen and had a career spanning 26 years with the fashion house. That show now feels particularly significant, as McGirr invited jeweller and former McQueen collaborator, Shaun Leane, to create pieces for the runway for the first time in 16 years, fulfilling a long-held ambition of his. McGirr was previously Head of Ready-to-wear at JW Anderson, the eponymous label of Magherafelt native Jonathan Anderson, now the Creative Director of Christian Dior. McGirr originally joined JW Anderson in 2020 to oversee men's collections, before taking on womenswear. McGirr is a graduate of Central Saint Martins where he obtained a Master of Arts in Fashion in 2014 and trained under Louise Wilson, an ambitious professor who mentored and influenced the careers of designers including Christopher Kane, Roksanda Ilincic and Mary Katrantzou.

stories.title: Ukraine strikes on Russia refineries 'a disgrace' - Trump
stories.summary: Ukraine's resumption of strikes on Russian refineries is a "disgrace" that keeps global energy prices elevated, US President Donald Trump has said. Ukraine struck a Russian oil refinery after President Volodymyr Zelensky declared that Kyiv was abandoning a ceasefire covering energy sites that Mr Trump had announced, and criticised his willingness to strike deals with Moscow. "All he's doing is making the world oil price higher. Well, I think that's a disgrace," Mr Trump told the Newsmax news outlet after Ukraine hit a Rosneft refinery southeast of Moscow which helps to supply the Russian capital. "There are a ‌lot of targets you ⁠can hit, but when you shoot at diesel refineries where you make, you know, diesel oil, and we need that, and the world needs that, then he's not doing a good service for the world," said Mr Trump. Russia rained down missile and drone strikes, targeting energy facilities such as power stations, knocking ‌out supply to hundreds of thousands, and Mr Zelensky told the Financial Times that Ukraine's patience had run out. Mr Trump's administration has ⁠been trying to mediate a ceasefire deal to end the war that started ‌with Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022.

stories.title: Fórsa awaiting formal Government approach on talks
stories.summary: Fórsa General Secretary Kevin Callinan has said there have been a lot "constructive inputs" today on public sector pay but they are still waiting for a formal approach from Government. He was speaking this evening following a meeting of the leaders of the four largest public sector unions Fórsa, SIPTU, the INMO and the INTO. It comes as Minister for Public Expenditure Jack Chambers has said he hopes to provide details "shortly" on "a way forward" on pay talks. Speaking in the Dáil during a Labour Party motion on pay talks, Minister Chambers said: "It may be possible to find a way forward shortly." Mr Callinan said he believes union members would expect a Government initiative that can restore trust and build confidence in public service industrial relations. "It needs an initiative. stories.title: Aontú to table no confidence motion in Helen McEntee
stories.summary: Aontú is to table a Dáil motion of no confidence in the Minister for Foreign Affairs Helen McEntee over her handling of garda whistleblower allegations. Aontú leader Peadar Tóibín confirmed his party will use its Dáil time on 4 November to bring forward the motion which will focus on Ms McEntee's tenure as Minister for Justice between 2020 and 2025. The programme revealed that two people who handled protected disclosures made by garda whistleblowers have themselves blown the whistle, alleging that reforms introduced to protect those who speak out have been undermined by senior management. They were among four garda whistleblowers speaking publicly for the first time in the programme. The Dáil heard claims that Ms McEntee "usurped the role" of the Office of the Protected Disclosure Commission by referring to An Garda Síochana a protected disclosure made to her. The Fine Gael Meath East TD rejected the claims, insisting she adhered to the law "at all times".

stories.title: AIB cuts 4-year fixed rate for mortgages over €250,000
stories.summary: AIB has today announced a cut of up to 0.35% on its four-year fixed rate for mortgages over €250,000. AIB said the new rate, which is available immediately for new and existing customers, will benefit those whose homes do not have a Building Energy Rating of B3 or higher. The bank said that customers are increasingly opting for the certainty of a competitively priced fixed rate after the ECB increased rates by 0.25% twice this year. Almost nine in ten new AIB customers have opted for a fixed rate this year, it noted. AIB said a monthly repayment on its new €350,000 AIB High Value 4-year fixed rate mortgage, with a loan to value of 50 to 80% over a 25-year term, will be €1,695.30. The previous monthly repayment would have been €1,750.82, representing a saving of €55.52 a month, €666.24 a year, or €4,715.72 over the 25-year term of the mortgage.

stories.title: Trump says gunman's execution will not be livestreamed
stories.summary: US President Donald Trump scrapped plans to livestream the execution of the former Army major who killed 13 people at Fort Hood, overruling Pentagon chief Pete Hegseth after the proposal drew opposition from Republicans, religious leaders and the public. The reversal ended a plan to broadcast Nidal Hasan's 3 December firing-squad execution. It also marked a rare public disagreement between Mr Trump and one of the president’s closest allies, although the Pentagon said the two were "completely aligned." Mr Hegseth had announced plans to livestream the execution at the Fort Hood military base in Texas, the site of Hasan's 2009 attack. No other country is known to televise or livestream judicial executions. Mr Trump and his advisers had been unaware of the livestream plan, said a White House official speaking on condition of anonymity.

stories.title: Bohemians lost the derby and the subsequent PR battle
stories.summary: There's rarely a dull week in the League of Ireland, but even by our own standards the last seven days have produced enough drama to fill a month's worth of headlines. Monday night's Dublin derby at Tallaght Stadium had everything we've come to expect from the biggest fixture in Irish football. A record league crowd in Tallaght Stadium of 10,208, three goals, controversy and some 'enjoyable' scenes following the final whistle. Shamrock Rovers' 2-1 victory has put them firmly in control of this title race. Dylan Watts' winner was a massive moment in their quest to keep hold of the trophy, but much of the conversation since has centred on the confrontation between both sets of players and staff. Four red cards followed, with Stephen Bradley subsequently making some strong accusations regarding the involvement of Bohemians staff in these incidents. Despite all this, Bohs' decided to maintain their media blackout. I understand their frustration with the fixture scheduling and the additional recovery time afforded to Rovers. Clubs are entitled to question decisions they believe are unfair.
stories.rssSummary: It is easy to understand Bohemians' frustration with the fixture scheduling, but persevering with a media ban following the contentious end to Monday's derby was unusual for a club normally so savvy in their communications, writes Eoin Doyle.

stories.title: Player of the month honour for Armagh star Mackin
stories.summary: Shane O'Neills history-maker Aimee Mackin has been honoured with The Croke Park Hotel/LGFA Player of the Month award for September. The Armagh star, who is also nominated for an All-Star and Players’ Player of the Year award, celebrated a landmark club success recently. The lethal 29-year-old attacker scored a remarkable tally of 1-12 in the Armagh county final last month as Shane O’Neills claimed the title for the very first time. That remarkable individual display followed on from a semi-final performance against Carrickcruppen, where she registered 3-05. The Shane O’Neills season continues next Sunday when they travel to Cavan champions Knockbride for their opening game in the round-robin phase of the Ulster championship. That game has a 2pm start at St Bridget’s Park in Knockbride. Remarkably, this is the fifth time that Aimee has claimed the Player of the Month award.

stories.title: Keane describes United as a 'circus' after Martinez rant
stories.summary: Roy Keane has branded Manchester United a "circus" following Lisandro Martinez's outburst against the club’s hierarchy. Argentina defender Martinez accused the club of lacking ambition and questioned their summer recruitment after Tuesday night’s 2-0 Champions League defeat by Atletico Madrid. Former United defender Gary Neville said Martinez’s comments amounted to a direct attack on his team-mates and suggested senior players would be "absolutely fuming", while ex-captain Keane described the remarks as symptomatic of the "chaos" at Old Trafford. "They’re obviously not together," Keane said of the club, speaking on The Overlap’s Stick to Football podcast. "It is chaotic there from the top to the bottom. We go there on match days and I don’t like the feeling around the club. "It just seems chaotic – statements can reflect it. It was chaotic with how they got to (Michael) Carrick as their manager. "We said from day one there were better options out there, and maybe the players are looking at there’s better options as players out there. It’s chaos, it’s like a circus."

stories.title: Lancaster voices maul concerns after scoring surge
stories.summary: Stuart Lancaster insists maul defence is Connacht's number one priority after the opening three games of the season, but is hoping to see a balance between how attacking and defending teams are refereed. The province have paid dearly for their maul struggles so far this season, with that areas of the game contributing significantly to the 12 tries they have conceded. They were mauled over their own line twice in the 22-19 win against Benetton earlier this month, while it happened four times in Friday night's defeat to Glasgow Warriors. Additionally, the province have picked up two yellow cards for maul infringements; Paul Boyle was sin-binned against Stormers in round one, during which time the South Africans took control of the game, while two of the five tries they conceded to Glasgow last week came during Sam Illo's yellow-card period. "Without stating the obvious, it's all stemmed from one aspect of the game, which was the rolling maul," Lancaster said, as he reflected on Connacht's struggles. And while he acknowledged his side have to be better at defending the maul, they also need to stop giving teams the opportunity to launch lineouts in the 22.

stories.title: Wexford Festival Opera - watch Iris by Pietro Mascagni
stories.summary: We proudly present a live presentation from this year's Wexford Festival Opera - Iris by Pietro Mascagni, with a libretto by Luigi Illica. Iris is a sensory feast and a rare opportunity to experience Italian opera at its most atmospheric and emotionally raw. Set not in a literal Japan, but a mythical one, it is a striking, symbolic masterpiece exploring the fragility of innocence in an uncaring world. Mascagni is best known for his first opera to be staged, Cavalleria rusticana, the work that changed operatic history by launching the verismo movement with panache and which opened in the Italian capital in 1890 to overwhelming acclaim. Iris – the fifth of his works to grace the Wexford stage – offers something more ethereal. Conducted by Francesco Cilluffo, whose reputation as a definitive interpreter of Mascagni's lush scores is further cemented by this, his third production of the composer’s work at the Festival. The opera invites us into the inner world of Iris, a young girl lured from her home into the city's dark pleasure quarters. A victim of societal corruption and exploitation, Iris remains luminous and untouched even as the world around her grows monstrous. She is a figure of tragic isolation – an object to be desired or judged, navigating a path toward a harrowing yet transcendent end. Musically staggering, powerful and provocative, Iris features one of the most dramatic choral sequences in the entire opera repertoire. The magnificent 'Hymn to the Sun’ bookends the opera, serving as both a powerful prologue and a redemptive, mystical epilogue. Find out more about this year's Wexford Festival Opera programme here

stories.title: Trans rights activists rush carpet at Harry Potter show
stories.summary: Several protesters campaigning for transgender rights rushed the red carpet ahead of the gala performance of Harry Potter And The Cursed Child in London on Thursday. The individuals, who wore masks and hats to conceal their identity, laid on the red carpet during the event at the Palace Theatre. The trans rights protesters were quickly removed by security, and one was wearing a t-shirt which said "Rowling money kills" which appeared to criticise JK Rowling, the author of the best-selling book series. The 61-year-old author has faced controversy in recent years because of her vocal stance on gender identity and has previously stated she thinks biological sex is "real" and "immutable". Rowling has also been critical of self-declared gender identity, calling it "quasi-religious" and "anti-science", but has denied being transphobic and previously said she respects "every trans person's right to live any way that feels authentic and comfortable to them". Her outspoken views have divided fans of the franchise and sparked a recent wave of protests and boycotts by trans rights activists targeting Harry Potter-themed events and locations.

stories.title: Things to do in Dublin this weekend (Oct 16-18)
stories.summary: From art exhibitions and Halloween markets to ponytail classes and scarecrow festivals, there is plenty happening in Dublin this weekend. Alternative Dublin is hosting an immersive, city-wide market this October as part of the Dublin Halloween Festival. Expect spoon ring makers, tattoo artists, tarot readers, vintage fashion, art, goody bags, prizes and much more. On Sunday, 18 October, the market will be taking place at Lost Lane from 12pm - 5pm. Free tickets will ensure access, but there may be a queue for entry depending on how busy they are! Please note that this market in Lost Lane is held upstairs and there is no lift access. Skerries Mills is a Community Heritage Centre at the heart of Skerries on the Dublin Coastal Trail. The visitor centre hosts a traditional cafe, craft shop, community gardens and much more. On Sunday, 18 October, they will have a family-friendly Scarecrow Festival running from 11am until 4.30pm. The National Gallery of Ireland is opening an exhibition developed in partnership with the Hilma af Klint Foundation. Open from 15 October 2026, and celebrating the work of one of Sweden's most celebrated modern artiststs, the exhibition features paintings, drawings and watercolours, and marks the first major monographic exhibition dedicated to the artist's work in Ireland. Living Loudly. Dying to be Heard: National Photography Exhibition launches this weekend, amplifying the voices of women living with advanced breast cancer. Taking place in Dundrum Town Centre on Saturday 17 and Sunday, 18 October, the photography exhibition features eight women from across Ireland sharing their stories of living with advanced breast cancer. The eight women featured are: Dr Tonya Leonard, Cynthia Cosme Cravo, Aine Murphy, Joy Keating, Barbara King, Fiona Dowd, Aileen O' Connor, and Hazel Fleming. Pints & Ponytails is a relaxed, social event that introduces dads to the world of hairstyling. KiwiCutz will demonstrate simple, everyday styles such as ponytails and easy braids using mannequin heads. There’s no cutting and no children present — just clear demos, practical tips, and time for questions. Taking place in the Storyteller pub on 18 October from 3pm - 4:30pm. Tickets €38.52.

stories.title: Man shot dead by loyalists settles action against PSNI
stories.summary: The family of a man shot dead on the way home from a GAA match in Croke Park during the Troubles have settled their civil action against the police. Sean Farmer, was 32 and a married father of five when he was gunned down by loyalists in August 1975. He and a work colleague were on their way back from the 1975 All-Ireland semi-final between Dublin and Derry when they were stopped at a bogus army checkpoint, near Newtownhamilton, Co Armagh. Both Mr Farmer and his workmate, 22-year-old Colm McCartney were shot dead on the side of the road. The Farmer family took a civil action against the police and the military. They claimed the then RUC had been guilty of malfeasance in a public office. They also claimed the killers included serving soldiers of the Ulster Defence Regiment.

stories.title: O'Donovan in intensive care after taking ill on Tuesday
stories.summary: Minister for Culture, Communications and Sport Patrick O'Donovan is in intensive care in hospital after falling ill earlier this week. It is understood he is being cared for at University Hospital Limerick. Mr O'Donovan was brought by ambulance to hospital after becoming unwell at an EU Presidency meeting at the University of Limerick (UL) on Tuesday. It is understood that he had a seizure. He was hospitalised over the summer after becoming unwell during an official trip to Brussels. The Limerick County TD has previously spoken about having been diagnosed with the neurological condition epilepsy. "We are praying he will be back shortly and that he will come through this and speedily get back to normal. He has so much to look forward to with the Ryder Cup coming to Limerick", said the Fine Gael councillor.

stories.title: Minister 'shocked' at UK decision on Sally Rooney books
stories.summary: Minister for Foreign Affairs Helen McEntee has said she was "shocked" that Sally Rooney's books are being removed from UK shops, and will raise the matter with her British counterpart. On Wednesday, Faber confirmed it will stop supplying Rooney's books in the UK, but says copies already held by retailers will not be removed from sale. Ms McEntee has told the Dáil she followed Rooney's work and held it in high regard. Minister McEntee also said she has spoken "a number of times" to her British counterpart, Ed Miliband, "who has set out very clearly" his position in support of Palestine. She said that she "has no problem" raising the matter of Ms Rooney with the UK Foreign Secretary, but cannot comment on another country's laws. She was responding to Social Democrats TD Sinéad Gibney who said that Ms Rooney is one of Ireland's most celebrated authors.

stories.title: Exports dip by 1.2% in August as trade figures normalise
stories.summary: New figures from the Central Statistics Office show that exports declined slightly in August, falling by 1.2% to €15.9 billion compared with €16 billion the same time last year. The CSO said the value of imports increased by 12.4% to €12.9 billion in August of this year compared with €11.5 billion in August of 2025. For the first eight months of the year, the CSO said that exports decreased by 23.9% to €138.4 billion, compared to the total of €181.8 billion the same time last year, when many companies were frontloading exports to the US due to concerns about tariffs. Meanwhile, the value of imports in the first eight months of 2026 increased by 13% to €12.3 billion from €106.9 billion. Today's figures show that Ireland's top exporting partners in August were the US, the Netherlands and Germany, with Ireland exporting 23.7%, 12.6% and 12.3% of total exports respectively to these countries. Meanwhile, Ireland imported the highest value of goods from the US, Great Britain and Germany with these countries representing 13.9%, 11% and 8.4% respectively of the total import trade for August.

stories.title: Police to re-open probe into handling of Linehan arrest
stories.summary: Police in the UK have been ordered to reinvestigate a complaint over the arrest of Father Ted co-creator Graham Linehan after a watchdog found failings in its handling of the case. The 58-year-old Irish writer was arrested at Heathrow Airport after flying in from Arizona in September 2025, on suspicion of inciting violence over three posts he made on X. He subsequently received an apology from police and a settlement following a civil claim. The Independent Office for Police Conduct (IOPC) confirmed Mr Linehan later sought a review of how police handled a complaint about the investigation into him and his treatment by officers. The application, received in May 2026, included "an allegation that he was discriminated against due to his gender-critical beliefs". The watchdog ruled the police's handling of Mr Linehan's complaint was inadequate and ordered the force to reinvestigate the allegation he had been discriminated against.

stories.title: Santry showcase puts two new rule tweaks in spotlight
stories.summary: Santry Avenue on a crisp October night provided the backdrop for football's latest rule tweaks to get one of their first competitive stress tests and the feedback would appear to be positive towards some of the new ideas being floated. UCD’s 9-19 to 1-09 hammering of Trinity College on Thursday in the opening round of the Higher Education Senior Football League may not live long in the memory, but it was significant in so far as, for the players and officials, they were operating with the new rules in a competitive fixture for the first time. The GAA’s Expert Advisory Group, led by Kevin McStay, has introduced a total of 11 rule modifications to be trialled over the course of the Higher Education Leagues this autumn. On the basis of what the modest attendance in north Dublin watched on Thursday evening, two in particular will dominate discussion above all others. The limit on consecutive hand-passes to three certainly appeared to encourage both sides to kick often and early, with UCD capable of flexing their muscles throughout a one-sided encounter by moving the ball quickly. There were a couple of infringements on both sides when it came to passing it a fourth time with a hand-pass, but it wasn’t as big a factor in the game as one might have expected pre-throw in. Players on both sides quite obviously counted the number of hand-passes aloud to ensure compliance with the new changes.
